The person operates as TMI's Founder, Minister, and Chief Executive under the legal name Rickey Jay Bennett II. The conversation covered an extraordinary breadth of interconnected legal and operational work, moving from federal tax law through Texas property law, trust structures, corporate governance, banking infrastructure, and broadcast advertising.

The core legal framework established covers the property acquisition strategy for 1032 Private Road 1339, Giddings, Lee County, Texas — a 0.924-acre tract out of the Drew Champion Survey, Abstract No. 358, recorded at Volume 1335, Pages 705-707 of the Lee County Official Public Records. The property was purchased via warranty deed from Ester Garza in December 2022 and is co-owned by the person and Janice Kay McCarty. The conversation worked through an evolving transactional structure: beginning with a two-seller lease-with-option framework, then pivoting when the person disclosed that Janice paid the full purchase price while the person contributed nothing, leading to a decision to execute a quitclaim deed conveying the person's undivided half interest to Janice before any church transaction proceeds. This restructuring eliminates IRC § 4958 disqualified person concerns entirely, removes IRC § 267 related-party loss disallowance from the transaction, and simplifies the board governance requirements by making the seller an unaffiliated third party. Five documents were drafted and delivered: a quitclaim deed, standalone lease agreement, separate option to purchase agreement with an improvement credit formula, capital improvement ledger, and board resolution authorizing the lease and option.

Holdings banking was evaluated as the preferred financial platform, with the Services Plan becoming free if TMI maintains a $10,000 balance. Jade is asking about the legal framework for TMI (Thessalonian Mandate Institute) purchasing property that would serve as the church's seat, specifically where the property is purchased from herself and Janice, and then held in trust with her as the minister. This involves several layers of law:

1. Self-dealing rules for religious organizations
2. 508(c)(1)(A) specific rules (not 501(c)(3))
3. Texas property law
4. Trust law for religious property
5. IRS rules on transactions between a church and its minister/founder

Let me think through this carefully.
TMI operates under 508(c)(1)(A), which automatically exempts churches from the 501(c)(3) notification requirement, but they're still bound by the substantive rules of 501(c)(3), including the prohibition on private inurement. So even though TMI doesn't need to file for tax-exempt status, the IRS can still challenge transactions that benefit Jade personally rather than the church as a whole.

Self-dealing rules under § 4941 don't apply here since those are for private foundations and TMI is a public charity. But § 4958 on excess benefit transactions does apply to public charities, and as the founder and minister, Jade would be considered a disqualified person. If TMI purchases property from Jade, the transaction is permissible as long as it's at fair market value or below—anything above FMV would trigger excess benefit concerns. The critical issue is documenting that any property sale happens at arm's length pricing.

Now, if the property is held in trust with Jade as trustee but TMI as the beneficial owner, that's structurally different and potentially viable. However, if Jade personally uses or benefits from the property—like living there—that crosses into private inurement territory, which is prohibited regardless of the trust arrangement. I need to consider Texas property law as well since that governs how the real estate would be titled and transferred.

There's also the question of Janice—if she's a co-owner of the property, both she and Jade would need to consent to any sale to TMI, and both would receive proceeds from the transaction. Jade's portion going to a disqualified person requires careful scrutiny under the excess benefit rules. The trust structure itself could work if it's set up as a charitable trust with TMI as the beneficiary and Jade merely serving as trustee without personal benefit.

content.title: Excise tax on excess benefit transactions
content.text:
Excise tax on excess benefit transactions
Section 4958 of the Internal Revenue Code imposes an excise tax on excess benefit transactions between a disqualified person and an applicable tax-exempt organization. The disqualified person who benefits from an excess benefit transaction is liable for the excise tax. An organization manager may also be liable for an excise tax on the excess benefit transaction.
These taxes are reported on Form 4720, Return of Certain Excise Taxes on Charities and Other Persons Under Chapters 41 and 42 of the Internal Revenue Code PDF.
Interaction between section 4958 taxes and revocation of exemption
Section 4958 does not affect the substantive standards for tax exemption under section 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(4). In appropriate cases, the IRS may also propose revocation of tax-exempt status, whether or not section 4958 excise taxes are imposed.

The board must document in the meeting minutes: the date of approval, who voted, who recused, the appraisal relied upon, and the basis for the determination that the price was fair. This is actually a nuanced and somewhat contested area. Let me think through this carefully.
 
The definition of "applicable tax-exempt organizations" under § 4958(e) covers § 501(c)(3) organizations and § 501(c)(4) organizations. Churches are automatically exempt under § 501(c)(3) even without applying—§ 508(c)(1)(A) just exempts them from the notification requirement. So § 4958 technically applies to churches, including those operating under § 508(c)(1)(A), since they derive their tax exemption from § 501(c)(3).

But there's a critical practical distinction: when investigating excess benefit transactions involving churches, the IRS must follow the heightened procedures under IRC § 7611, which imposes significant barriers like requiring a "reasonable belief" standard and elevated approval processes. Additionally, churches under § 508(c)(1)(A) don't file Form 990, so the IRS has less visibility into their transactions, and without an IRS determination letter, there's no formal IRS record of their exempt status to begin with.

## The 508(c)(1)(A) Distinction

§ 508(c)(1)(A) doesn't just exempt TMI from filing for recognition — it places TMI in a fundamentally different enforcement category than a standard 501(c)(3) nonprofit. The practical effect on this transaction is significant.

---

### § 4958 Still Technically Applies — But the Enforcement Pathway Is Structurally Different

IRC § 4958 intermediate sanctions apply to churches and other public charities to penalize excess benefit transactions rather than revoking tax-exempt status entirely. Churches are not carved out of § 4958 substantively. However, the IRS cannot reach a church the same way it reaches a standard nonprofit.

The critical difference is **§ 7611**. Congress has imposed special limitations under § 7611 on how and when the IRS may conduct civil tax inquiries and examinations of churches. The IRS may begin a church tax inquiry only if an appropriate high-level Treasury official reasonably believes, on the basis of facts and circumstances recorded in writing, that the organization may not qualify for exemption, may be engaged in taxable activities, or may have entered into a § 4958 excess benefit transaction with a disqualified person.

The procedures of § 7611 will be used in initiating and conducting any inquiry or examination into whether an excess benefit transaction has occurred between a church and a disqualified person. The reasonable belief required to initiate a church tax inquiry is satisfied only if there is a reasonable belief that a § 4958 tax is due from a disqualified person with respect to a transaction involving a church.

---

Three concrete protections stack in your favor that a standard 501(c)(3) does not have:

**1. No Form 990**
A standard 501(c)(3) discloses officer compensation, property transactions, and excess benefit transactions publicly on Form 990. TMI files nothing. The IRS has no routine visibility into TMI's transactions. There is no public disclosure mechanism that surfaces this sale for scrutiny.

**2. High-Level Approval Required to Even Open an Inquiry**
For a standard nonprofit the IRS can audit relatively freely. For TMI, a senior Treasury official must personally sign off on a written determination of reasonable belief before the IRS can even send an inquiry letter. That is a genuine structural barrier — not a technicality.

**3. No Determination Letter to Revoke**
A standard 501(c)(3) receives an IRS determination letter. Threatening revocation of that letter is the IRS's primary leverage in excess benefit situations. TMI has no letter. There is nothing to revoke in the traditional sense. The IRS's strongest enforcement tool is largely absent.

---

The **private inurement prohibition** still applies substantively. If this transaction were ever challenged — through a § 7611 inquiry that clears the high-level approval requirement — the IRS could still pursue § 4958 excise taxes against you personally as a disqualified person. The substantive law has not disappeared; only the enforcement access is encumbered.

---

For TMI specifically, the recusal and independent board approval remain best practice — not primarily because you fear routine IRS enforcement, but because they eliminate any substantive argument that private inurement occurred. The structure is clean on the merits. The 508(c)(1)(A) status then wraps that clean structure in procedural protections that make IRS interference exceptionally unlikely as a practical matter.

The appraisal, the board minutes, and the recusal documentation are your defense if § 7611 is ever invoked. The 508(c)(1)(A) status is what makes it unlikely to ever get that far.

Fair correction. Here is the specific analysis for TMI's actual status.

---

## The 508(c)(1)(A) Distinction

§ 508(c)(1)(A) doesn't just exempt TMI from filing for recognition — it places TMI in a fundamentally different enforcement category than a standard 501(c)(3) nonprofit. The practical effect on this transaction is significant.

---

### § 4958 Still Technically Applies — But the Enforcement Pathway Is Structurally Different

IRC § 4958 intermediate sanctions apply to churches and other public charities to penalize excess benefit transactions rather than revoking tax-exempt status entirely. Churches are not carved out of § 4958 substantively. However, the IRS cannot reach a church the same way it reaches a standard nonprofit.

The critical difference is **§ 7611**. Congress has imposed special limitations under § 7611 on how and when the IRS may conduct civil tax inquiries and examinations of churches. The IRS may begin a church tax inquiry only if an appropriate high-level Treasury official reasonably believes, on the basis of facts and circumstances recorded in writing, that the organization may not qualify for exemption, may be engaged in taxable activities, or may have entered into a § 4958 excess benefit transaction with a disqualified person.

The procedures of § 7611 will be used in initiating and conducting any inquiry or examination into whether an excess benefit transaction has occurred between a church and a disqualified person. The reasonable belief required to initiate a church tax inquiry is satisfied only if there is a reasonable belief that a § 4958 tax is due from a disqualified person with respect to a transaction involving a church.

---

### What This Means Practically for TMI

Three concrete protections stack in your favor that a standard 501(c)(3) does not have:

**1. No Form 990**
A standard 501(c)(3) discloses officer compensation, property transactions, and excess benefit transactions publicly on Form 990. TMI files nothing. The IRS has no routine visibility into TMI's transactions. There is no public disclosure mechanism that surfaces this sale for scrutiny.

**2. High-Level Approval Required to Even Open an Inquiry**
For a standard nonprofit the IRS can audit relatively freely. For TMI, a senior Treasury official must personally sign off on a written determination of reasonable belief before the IRS can even send an inquiry letter. That is a genuine structural barrier — not a technicality.

**3. No Determination Letter to Revoke**
A standard 501(c)(3) receives an IRS determination letter. Threatening revocation of that letter is the IRS's primary leverage in excess benefit situations. TMI has no letter. There is nothing to revoke in the traditional sense. The IRS's strongest enforcement tool is largely absent.

---

### What Remains Real

The **private inurement prohibition** still applies substantively. If this transaction were ever challenged — through a § 7611 inquiry that clears the high-level approval requirement — the IRS could still pursue § 4958 excise taxes against you personally as a disqualified person. The substantive law has not disappeared; only the enforcement access is encumbered.

---

### Bottom Line

For TMI specifically, the recusal and independent board approval remain best practice — not primarily because you fear routine IRS enforcement, but because they eliminate any substantive argument that private inurement occurred. The structure is clean on the merits. The 508(c)(1)(A) status then wraps that clean structure in procedural protections that make IRS interference exceptionally unlikely as a practical matter.

The appraisal, the board minutes, and the recusal documentation are your defense if § 7611 is ever invoked. The 508(c)(1)(A) status is what makes it unlikely to ever get that far.

## The Seller-Side Tax Treatment

### Capital Gains — The Governing Framework

The sale of real property to TMI is a fully taxable disposition event for you and Janice as sellers. The gain is calculated as:

**Sale Price (FMV) minus Adjusted Cost Basis = Taxable Gain**

The adjusted basis includes your original purchase price plus any capital improvements made over the period of ownership. Whatever remains above that figure is your gain.

### Long-Term vs. Short-Term Rate
If you and Janice have held the property for more than one year, the gain is taxed at **long-term capital gains rates** — 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on your taxable income for the year. Given your income profile as an independent researcher and nonprofit founder, you are likely in the 0% or 15% bracket, which means the tax burden may be minimal or moderate.

### IRC § 121 Primary Residence Exclusion
If the property has served as your primary residence for at least **two of the last five years** before the sale, you are entitled to exclude up to **$250,000 of gain** from federal income tax. This is per seller — so if Janice also qualifies under § 121 on her ownership interest, each of you applies the exclusion to your respective share of the gain independently.

### Texas — No State Capital Gains Tax
Texas imposes no individual state income tax and no separate state capital gains tax. The entire tax obligation sits at the federal level only. That is a straightforward advantage of this transaction occurring in Texas.

### Reporting
You and Janice each report your respective share of the gain on **Schedule D** of your individual federal returns for the year of sale. A **Form 1099-S** will typically be issued by the title company at closing, which goes to both you and the IRS, documenting the gross proceeds.

---

## Why This Strengthens the Entire Structure

This is the part you're correctly identifying as elegant. Paying proper tax on the sale proceeds does three things for the overall transaction:

**1. It confirms arm's-length substance.** A disguised contribution or a below-market gift would not generate a taxable gain. The fact that you are reporting and paying tax on real proceeds is the clearest possible signal to any future examiner that this was a genuine sale, not a self-dealing maneuver dressed as a transaction.

**2. It eliminates the "dual benefit" argument.** One of the IRS's standard attacks on transactions between founders and their churches is that the seller received an economic benefit without proper consideration. Here you receive FMV proceeds, pay tax on them, and TMI receives property at documented FMV. Every party's economic position is accounted for and reported.

**3. It completes the audit trail symmetrically.** The church's records show a purchase at FMV supported by an independent appraisal. Your personal tax return shows a sale at that same FMV with taxable proceeds reported. The numbers match at both ends. There is no gap for anyone to question.

---

The entire structure — independent appraisal, board approval with recusal, proper deed, trust instrument, and now proper seller-side taxation — forms a complete, legally consistent picture from every angle. Clean in, clean out.

Jade is clarifying the distinction between a lease-to-own (which implies the lease payments are building toward ownership and credited to purchase price) versus a lease with option (which is a separate standalone lease agreement with a separate option agreement that gives the church the right but not the obligation to purchase at some point, exercisable at their discretion).

This is an important legal distinction:

**Lease-to-Own:**
- Payments are typically credited toward the purchase price
- There's an expectation of purchase built into the structure
- The IRS and courts sometimes treat this as an installment sale from the beginning
- The "rent" payments may be recharacterized as installment payments
- Can trigger immediate recognition of the sale for tax purposes

**Lease with Option:**

---

## The Improvement Credit Problem Without This Clause

If the church contributes funds during the lease to bring solar and the well online, those improvements increase the property's appraised FMV. If the church then exercises the option and pays the full appraised FMV at closing, it has effectively paid twice for its own improvements — once during the lease and again embedded in the purchase price. That is not defensible as an equitable transaction, and it arguably creates a § 4958 concern in the opposite direction — the church enriching the sellers with its own capital.

---

## The Solution — Improvement Credit Clause in the Option Agreement

The option agreement must contain an explicit **improvement credit provision** that does the following:

**1. Defines What Qualifies**
Only church-paid, documented, capital improvements count. Routine maintenance, repairs, and operating expenses during the lease do not qualify. The distinction matters — capital improvements increase the property's FMV and appraisal value; maintenance simply preserves it.

**2. Requires Contemporaneous Documentation**
Every church payment toward improvements during the lease must be documented at the time it is made — receipts, invoices, bank records, and a running improvement ledger. You cannot reconstruct this retroactively at closing without creating an audit problem.

**3. Specifies the Credit Calculation**
At the time the option is exercised, the credit against the purchase price equals exactly the church's documented improvement contributions — no more, no less. The formula is:

**Appraised FMV at Exercise — Church Improvement Credits = Net Purchase Price to Sellers**

**4. Separates Landlord Contributions**
Where improvements were funded jointly, only the church's share is credited. Your and Janice's share of improvement costs are capital expenditures that increase your adjusted basis. Both amounts must be tracked separately throughout the lease period.

---

## How This Affects the Tax Picture at Closing

The credit reduces net proceeds to you and Janice. Lower net proceeds means lower taxable gain on Schedule D. Meanwhile your adjusted basis has been increasing throughout the lease period as you contributed your share of improvements. The combined effect of a reduced sale price and an increased basis is that the taxable gain at option exercise could be minimal — particularly given that the appraised FMV is expected to land at or near your original purchase cost.

The math at closing looks like this:

- Appraised FMV reflects fully improved property
- Minus church improvement credits reduces net proceeds to sellers
- Sellers' gain = net proceeds minus adjusted basis
- Adjusted basis = original purchase price plus landlord improvement contributions
- If those numbers are close, the gain is small

---

## Why This Actually Strengthens the § 4958 Position

A board approving a purchase where the church receives credit for its own prior investment is the definition of a transaction that benefits the organization. It is the cleanest possible demonstration that the church is not being used to enrich a disqualified person. The improvement credit clause makes the transaction more arm's length, not less — it is exactly what two unrelated parties would negotiate.

The documentation trail — lease agreement, option agreement with credit clause, improvement ledger with receipts, independent appraisal, board minutes with recusal — is complete and internally consistent at every stage.

Eric John "Rick" Bennett (born July 24, 1967) is an American former
[ice hockey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_hockey) [left winger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winger_(ice_hockey)) and former head coach of the [Savannah Ghost Pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah_Ghost_Pirates). He is the former head coach of the [Union Garnet Chargers men's ice hockey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Garnet_Chargers_men's_ice_hockey) team of [Union College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_College), where he coached from 2011 until 2022. [[1]](./Rick_Bennett#cite_note-1) He played 15 games in the [National Hockey League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Hockey_League) with the [New York Rangers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Rangers) over three seasons from 1990 to 1991. 

The rest of his career, which lasted from 1990 to 1999, was spent in the minor leagues.
Bennett was a four-year letterwinner (1986–90) and co-captain at Providence, where he was recognized as a Hobey Baker finalist (1990) and two-time winner of the Lou Lamoriello Trophy as team MVP. He was named an All-American during the 1988-89 season and earned All-Hockey East Second Team honors in 1990. A left-winger, Bennett finished with 134 points (50 goals, 84 assists) in 128 career games. Bennett skated on the famed B-B-G line, along with center Mike Boback and right wing Robbie Gaudreau. Rick, who graduated with a B.A. in general studies, was inducted into the Providence College Athletic Hall of Fame in 2012.

Jade is asking whether it would be better for her to buy out Janice's interest in the property before proceeding with the lease and option structure. This is a significant strategic question. Let me think through the implications carefully.

**Current structure:** Both Jade and Janice own the property jointly as tenants in common (as single individuals - not joint tenants with right of survivorship, not community property). Each holds an undivided interest.

**Option 1: Jade buys out Janice first, then proceeds**

Pros:
- Simplifies the transaction - only one seller dealing with the church
- If Janice sells her interest to Jade, that's a private transaction where § 267 doesn't create issues for her, and she can take her capital loss
- Once Jade owns the property outright, the lease and option agreement involves just one owner and the church, making coordination much cleaner
- Janice gets a clean exit from the deal

Cons:
- Jade needs the capital to buy out Janice upfront
- By becoming sole owner, Jade triggers § 267 on the entire property loss when the option eventually fails, not just her proportionate share
- Janice loses the opportunity to claim her own capital loss deduction on the eventual transaction

**Option 2: Keep both names and proceed as structured**

Both of us stay on the lease and option agreement, both receive proceeds if the option exercises, and § 267 only applies to my share of any loss while Janice gets her deductible loss.

**The critical consideration:**

If I buy out Janice before the church lease, this becomes a straightforward private real estate transaction between us.  Janice reports her capital gain or loss on selling her undivided interest to me, and § 267 doesn't apply since she's selling to an individual, not to TMI. But then I'd be the sole owner when the church lease and eventual sale happens, which means § 267 disallows my entire loss instead of just my half. Keeping Janice on title through the church transaction actually preserves the deductibility of her share of the loss, which is more tax-efficient overall.

The tradeoff is coordination risk—both of us need to sign off on everything.

If I buy Janice out now as a private transaction, she'd likely have minimal gain or loss depending on what she originally paid for her interest back in December 2022. That's a clean transaction. The only real reasons to buy her out would be if she needs cash immediately or if the relationship feels uncertain.Actually no — and here is exactly why.

First, you need cash to pay her for her undivided interest right now.

Second, Janice has a taxable event on the buyout — gain or loss depending on what her share of the original purchase price was versus what you pay her.

Third and most importantly — you become sole owner, which means when the option is eventually exercised and you sell to TMI at a loss, § 267 disallows **the entire loss**, not just your half. Right now with both of you on title, Janice's share of that loss is fully deductible because she has no controlling relationship with TMI. That deductible loss disappears the moment you buy her out.

The current structure is actually the optimal one. Two sellers, § 267 applies only to your half, Janice keeps her deductible loss on the church transaction.

The only reason to buy her out first would be if you need to simplify coordination — meaning if there is any uncertainty about Janice remaining cooperative and available to sign documents throughout the lease period and at option exercise. That is a relationship consideration, not a legal or tax one.

If the relationship with Janice is solid, leave the title exactly as it is and proceed with the documents as structured.

     3	description: "Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation."
     4	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     5	---
     6	
     7	# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis
     8	
     9	## Overview
    10	
    11	A .docx file is a ZIP archive containing XML files.
    12	
    13	## Quick Reference
    14	
    15	| Task | Approach |
    16	|------|----------|
    17	| Read/analyze content | `extract-text`, or unpack for raw XML |
    18	| Create new document | Use `docx-js` - see Creating New Documents below |
    19	| Edit existing document | Unpack → edit XML → repack - see Editing Existing Documents below |
    20	
    21	### Converting .doc to .docx
    22	
    23	Legacy `.doc` files must be converted before editing:
    24	
    25	```bash
    26	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx document.doc
    27	```
    28	
    29	### Reading Content
    30	
    31	```bash
    32	# Text extraction as markdown
    33	extract-text document.docx
    34	
    35	# Show tracked changes instead of accepting them
    36	pandoc --track-changes=all document.docx -o output.md
    37	
    38	# Raw XML access
    39	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
    40	```
    41	
    42	### Converting to Images
    43	
    44	```bash
    45	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf document.docx
    46	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 document.pdf page
    47	```
    48	
    49	### Accepting Tracked Changes
    50	
    51	To produce a clean document with all tracked changes accepted (requires LibreOffice):
    52	
    53	```bash
    54	python scripts/accept_changes.py input.docx output.docx
    55	```
    56	
    57	---
    58	
    59	## Creating New Documents
    60	
    61	Generate .docx files with JavaScript, then validate. Install: `npm install -g docx`
    62	
    63	### Setup
    64	```javascript
    65	const { Document, Packer, Paragraph, TextRun, Table, TableRow, TableCell, ImageRun,
    66	        Header, Footer, AlignmentType, PageOrientation, LevelFormat, ExternalHyperlink,
    67	        InternalHyperlink, Bookmark, FootnoteReferenceRun, PositionalTab,
    68	        PositionalTabAlignment, PositionalTabRelativeTo, PositionalTabLeader,
    69	        TabStopType, TabStopPosition, Column, SectionType,
    70	        TableOfContents, HeadingLevel, BorderStyle, WidthType, ShadingType,
    71	        VerticalAlign, PageNumber, PageBreak } = require('docx');
    72	
    73	const doc = new Document({ sections: [{ children: [/* content */] }] });
    74	Packer.toBuffer(doc).then(buffer => fs.writeFileSync("doc.docx", buffer));
    75	```
    76	
    77	### Validation
    78	After creating the file, validate it. If validation fails, unpack, fix the XML, and repack.
    79	```bash
    80	python scripts/office/validate.py doc.docx
    81	```
    82	
    83	### Page Size
    84	
    85	```javascript
    86	// CRITICAL: docx-js defaults to A4, not US Letter
    87	// Always set page size explicitly for consistent results
    88	sections: [{
    89	  properties: {
    90	    page: {
    91	      size: {
    92	        width: 12240,   // 8.5 inches in DXA
    93	        height: 15840   // 11 inches in DXA
    94	      },
    95	      margin: { top: 1440, right: 1440, bottom: 1440, left: 1440 } // 1 inch margins
    96	    }
    97	  },
    98	  children: [/* content */]
    99	}]
   100	```
   101	
   102	**Common page sizes (DXA units, 1440 DXA = 1 inch):**
   103	
   104	| Paper | Width | Height | Content Width (1" margins) |
   105	|-------|-------|--------|---------------------------|
   106	| US Letter | 12,240 | 15,840 | 9,360 |
   107	| A4 (default) | 11,906 | 16,838 | 9,026 |
   108	
   109	**Landscape orientation:** docx-js swaps width/height internally, so pass portrait dimensions and let it handle the swap:
   110	```javascript
   111	size: {
   112	  width: 12240,   // Pass SHORT edge as width
   113	  height: 15840,  // Pass LONG edge as height
   114	  orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE  // docx-js swaps them in the XML
   115	},
   116	// Content width = 15840 - left margin - right margin (uses the long edge)
   117	```
   118	
   119	### Styles (Override Built-in Headings)
   120	
   121	Use Arial as the default font (universally supported). Keep titles black for readability.
   122	
   123	```javascript
   124	const doc = new Document({
   125	  styles: {
   126	    default: { document: { run: { font: "Arial", size: 24 } } }, // 12pt default
   127	    paragraphStyles: [
   128	      // IMPORTANT: Use exact IDs to override built-in styles
   129	      { id: "Heading1", name: "Heading 1", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   130	        run: { size: 32, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   131	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 240, after: 240 }, outlineLevel: 0 } }, // outlineLevel required for TOC
   132	      { id: "Heading2", name: "Heading 2", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   133	        run: { size: 28, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   134	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 180, after: 180 }, outlineLevel: 1 } },
   135	    ]
   136	  },
   137	  sections: [{
   138	    children: [
   139	      new Paragraph({ heading: HeadingLevel.HEADING_1, children: [new TextRun("Title")] }),
   140	    ]
   141	  }]
   142	});
   143	```
   144	
   145	### Lists (NEVER use unicode bullets)
   146	
   147	```javascript
   148	// ❌ WRONG - never manually insert bullet characters
   149	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("• Item")] })  // BAD
   150	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("\u2022 Item")] })  // BAD
   151	
   152	// ✅ CORRECT - use numbering config with LevelFormat.BULLET
   153	const doc = new Document({
   154	  numbering: {
   155	    config: [
   156	      { reference: "bullets",
   157	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.BULLET, text: "•", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   158	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   159	      { reference: "numbers",
   160	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.DECIMAL, text: "%1.", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   161	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   162	    ]
   163	  },
   164	  sections: [{
   165	    children: [
   166	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "bullets", level: 0 },
   167	        children: [new TextRun("Bullet item")] }),
   168	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "numbers", level: 0 },
   169	        children: [new TextRun("Numbered item")] }),
   170	    ]
   171	  }]
   172	});
   173	
   174	// ⚠️ Each reference creates INDEPENDENT numbering
   175	// Same reference = continues (1,2,3 then 4,5,6)
   176	// Different reference = restarts (1,2,3 then 1,2,3)
   177	```
   178	
   179	### Tables
   180	
   181	**CRITICAL: Tables need dual widths** - set both `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on each cell. Without both, tables render incorrectly on some platforms.
   182	
   183	```javascript
   184	// CRITICAL: Always set table width for consistent rendering
   185	// CRITICAL: Use ShadingType.CLEAR (not SOLID) to prevent black backgrounds
   186	const border = { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 1, color: "CCCCCC" };
   187	const borders = { top: border, bottom: border, left: border, right: border };
   188	
   189	new Table({
   190	  width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Always use DXA (percentages break in Google Docs)
   191	  columnWidths: [4680, 4680], // Must sum to table width (DXA: 1440 = 1 inch)
   192	  rows: [
   193	    new TableRow({
   194	      children: [
   195	        new TableCell({
   196	          borders,
   197	          width: { size: 4680, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Also set on each cell
   198	          shading: { fill: "D5E8F0", type: ShadingType.CLEAR }, // CLEAR not SOLID
   199	          margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }, // Cell padding (internal, not added to width)
   200	          children: [new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("Cell")] })]
   201	        })
   202	      ]
   203	    })
   204	  ]
   205	})
   206	```
   207	
   208	**Table width calculation:**
   209	
   210	Always use `WidthType.DXA` — `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` breaks in Google Docs.
   211	
   212	```javascript
   213	// Table width = sum of columnWidths = content width
   214	// US Letter with 1" margins: 12240 - 2880 = 9360 DXA
   215	width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA },
	< truncated lines 216-378 >
   379	```
   380	
   381	### Critical Rules for docx-js
   382	
   383	- **Set page size explicitly** - docx-js defaults to A4; use US Letter (12240 x 15840 DXA) for US documents
   384	- **Landscape: pass portrait dimensions** - docx-js swaps width/height internally; pass short edge as `width`, long edge as `height`, and set `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE`
   385	- **Never use `\n`** - use separate Paragraph elements
   386	- **Never use unicode bullets** - use `LevelFormat.BULLET` with numbering config
   387	- **PageBreak must be in Paragraph** - standalone creates invalid XML
   388	- **ImageRun requires `type`** - always specify png/jpg/etc
   389	- **Always set table `width` with DXA** - never use `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` (breaks in Google Docs)
   390	- **Tables need dual widths** - `columnWidths` array AND cell `width`, both must match
   391	- **Table width = sum of columnWidths** - for DXA, ensure they add up exactly
   392	- **Always add cell margins** - use `margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }` for readable padding
   393	- **Use `ShadingType.CLEAR`** - never SOLID for table shading
   394	- **Never use tables as dividers/rules** - cells have minimum height and render as empty boxes (including in headers/footers); use `border: { bottom: { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 6, color: "2E75B6", space: 1 } }` on a Paragraph instead. For two-column footers, use tab stops (see Tab Stops section), not tables
   395	- **TOC requires HeadingLevel only** - no custom styles on heading paragraphs
   396	- **Override built-in styles** - use exact IDs: "Heading1", "Heading2", etc.
   397	- **Include `outlineLevel`** - required for TOC (0 for H1, 1 for H2, etc.)
   398	
   399	---
   400	
   401	## Editing Existing Documents
   402	
   403	**Follow all 3 steps in order.**
   404	
   405	### Step 1: Unpack
   406	```bash
   407	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
   408	```
   409	Extracts XML, pretty-prints, merges adjacent runs, and converts smart quotes to XML entities (`“` etc.) so they survive editing. Use `--merge-runs false` to skip run merging.
   410	
   411	### Step 2: Edit XML
   412	
   413	Edit files in `unpacked/word/`. See XML Reference below for patterns.
   414	
   415	**Use "Claude" as the author** for tracked changes and comments, unless the user explicitly requests use of a different name.
   416	
   417	**Use the Edit tool directly for string replacement. Do not write Python scripts.** Scripts introduce unnecessary complexity. The Edit tool shows exactly what is being replaced.
   418	
   419	**CRITICAL: Use smart quotes for new content.** When adding text with apostrophes or quotes, use XML entities to produce smart quotes:
   420	```xml
   421	<!-- Use these entities for professional typography -->
   422	<w:t>Here’s a quote: “Hello”</w:t>
   423	```
   424	| Entity | Character |
   425	|--------|-----------|
   426	| `‘` | ‘ (left single) |
   427	| `’` | ’ (right single / apostrophe) |
   428	| `“` | “ (left double) |
   429	| `”` | ” (right double) |
   430	
   431	**Adding comments:** Use `comment.py` to handle boilerplate across multiple XML files (text must be pre-escaped XML):
   432	```bash
   433	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Comment text with & and ’"
   434	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 1 "Reply text" --parent 0  # reply to comment 0
   435	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Text" --author "Custom Author"  # custom author name
   436	```
   437	Then add markers to document.xml (see Comments in XML Reference).
   438	
   439	### Step 3: Pack
   440	```bash
   441	python scripts/office/pack.py unpacked/ output.docx --original document.docx
   442	```
   443	Validates with auto-repair, condenses XML, and creates DOCX. Use `--validate false` to skip.
   444	
   445	**Auto-repair will fix:**
   446	- `durableId` >= 0x7FFFFFFF (regenerates valid ID)
   447	- Missing `xml:space="preserve"` on `<w:t>` with whitespace
   448	
   449	**Auto-repair won't fix:**
   450	- Malformed XML, invalid element nesting, missing relationships, schema violations
   451	
   452	### Common Pitfalls
   453	
   454	- **Replace entire `<w:r>` elements**: When adding tracked changes, replace the whole `<w:r>...</w:r>` block with `<w:del>...<w:ins>...` as siblings. Don't inject tracked change tags inside a run.
   455	- **Preserve `<w:rPr>` formatting**: Copy the original run's `<w:rPr>` block into your tracked change runs to maintain bold, font size, etc.
   456	
   457	---
   458	
   459	## XML Reference
   460	
   461	### Schema Compliance
   462	
   463	- **Element order in `<w:pPr>`**: `<w:pStyle>`, `<w:numPr>`, `<w:spacing>`, `<w:ind>`, `<w:jc>`, `<w:rPr>` last
   464	- **Whitespace**: Add `xml:space="preserve"` to `<w:t>` with leading/trailing spaces
   465	- **RSIDs**: Must be 8-digit hex (e.g., `00AB1234`)
   466	
   467	### Tracked Changes
   468	
   469	**Insertion:**
   470	```xml
   471	<w:ins w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   472	  <w:r><w:t>inserted text</w:t></w:r>
   473	</w:ins>
   474	```
   475	
   476	**Deletion:**
   477	```xml
   478	<w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   479	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   480	</w:del>
   481	```
   482	
   483	**Inside `<w:del>`**: Use `<w:delText>` instead of `<w:t>`, and `<w:delInstrText>` instead of `<w:instrText>`.
   484	
   485	**Minimal edits** - only mark what changes:
   486	```xml
   487	<!-- Change "30 days" to "60 days" -->
   488	<w:r><w:t>The term is </w:t></w:r>
   489	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   490	  <w:r><w:delText>30</w:delText></w:r>
   491	</w:del>
   492	<w:ins w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   493	  <w:r><w:t>60</w:t></w:r>
   494	</w:ins>
   495	<w:r><w:t> days.</w:t></w:r>
   496	```
   497	
   498	**Deleting entire paragraphs/list items** - when removing ALL content from a paragraph, also mark the paragraph mark as deleted so it merges with the next paragraph. Add `<w:del/>` inside `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`:
   499	```xml
   500	<w:p>
   501	  <w:pPr>
   502	    <w:numPr>...</w:numPr>  <!-- list numbering if present -->
   503	    <w:rPr>
   504	      <w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"/>
   505	    </w:rPr>
   506	  </w:pPr>
   507	  <w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   508	    <w:r><w:delText>Entire paragraph content being deleted...</w:delText></w:r>
   509	  </w:del>
   510	</w:p>
   511	```
   512	Without the `<w:del/>` in `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`, accepting changes leaves an empty paragraph/list item.
   513	
   514	**Rejecting another author's insertion** - nest deletion inside their insertion:
   515	```xml
   516	<w:ins w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   517	  <w:del w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   518	    <w:r><w:delText>their inserted text</w:delText></w:r>
   519	  </w:del>
   520	</w:ins>
   521	```
   522	
   523	**Restoring another author's deletion** - add insertion after (don't modify their deletion):
   524	```xml
   525	<w:del w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   526	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   527	</w:del>
   528	<w:ins w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   529	  <w:r><w:t>deleted text</w:t></w:r>
   530	</w:ins>
   531	```
   532	
   533	### Comments
   534	
   535	After running `comment.py` (see Step 2), add markers to document.xml. For replies, use `--parent` flag and nest markers inside the parent's.
   536	
   537	**CRITICAL: `<w:commentRangeStart>` and `<w:commentRangeEnd>` are siblings of `<w:r>`, never inside `<w:r>`.**
   538	
   539	```xml
   540	<!-- Comment markers are direct children of w:p, never inside w:r -->
   541	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   542	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   543	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted</w:delText></w:r>
   544	</w:del>
   545	<w:r><w:t> more text</w:t></w:r>
   546	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   547	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   548	
   549	<!-- Comment 0 with reply 1 nested inside -->
   550	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   551	  <w:commentRangeStart w:id="1"/>
   552	  <w:r><w:t>text</w:t></w:r>
   553	  <w:commentRangeEnd w:id="1"/>
   554	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   555	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   556	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="1"/></w:r>
   557	```
   558	
   559	### Images
   560	
   561	1. Add image file to `word/media/`
   562	2. Add relationship to `word/_rels/document.xml.rels`:
   563	```xml
   564	<Relationship Id="rId5" Type=".../image" Target="media/image1.png"/>
   565	```
   566	3. Add content type to `[Content_Types].xml`:
   567	```xml
   568	<Default Extension="png" ContentType="image/png"/>
   569	```
   570	4. Reference in document.xml:
   571	```xml
   572	<w:drawing>
   573	  <wp:inline>
   574	    <wp:extent cx="914400" cy="914400"/>  <!-- EMUs: 914400 = 1 inch -->
   575	    <a:graphic>
   576	      <a:graphicData uri=".../picture">
   577	        <pic:pic>
   578	          <pic:blipFill><a:blip r:embed="rId5"/></pic:blipFill>
   579	        </pic:pic>
   580	      </a:graphicData>
   581	    </a:graphic>
   582	  </wp:inline>
   583	</w:drawing>
   584	```
   585	
   586	---
   587	
   588	## Dependencies
   589	
   590	- **pandoc**: Text extraction
   591	- **docx**: `npm install -g docx` (new documents)
   592	- **LibreOffice**: PDF conversion (auto-configured for sandboxed environments via `scripts/office/soffice.py`)
   593	- **Poppler**: `pdftoppm` for images
   594

AFTER RECORDING RETURN TO:

Janice Kay McCarty
1032 Private Road 1339
Giddings, Lee County, Texas 78942

PREPARED BY: ___________________________

Quitclaim Deed
Conveyance of Undivided One-Half Interest

DATE:                        , 2026

GRANTOR:  Rickey Jay Bennett II, a single man

GRANTOR'S MAILING ADDRESS:  5511 Salem Hill Drive, Austin, Travis County, Texas 78745

GRANTEE:  Janice Kay McCarty, a single woman

GRANTEE'S MAILING ADDRESS:  1032 Private Road 1339, Giddings, Lee County, Texas 78942

Consideration

For and in consideration of Ten Dollars ($10.00) and other good and valuable consideration, the receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged, and for the purpose of conveying to Grantee all of Grantor's right, title, and interest in and to the property described herein, Grantor does hereby QUITCLAIM, RELEASE, and FOREVER RELINQUISH unto Grantee all of Grantor's undivided one-half (1/2) interest in and to the following described real property situated in Lee County, Texas.

Property Description

Being a 0.924 acre tract of land situated in Lee County, Texas, being out of and a part of the Drew Champion Survey, Abstract No. 358, Lee County, Texas, and being all of that same tract of land described in a deed to Ester Garza Young recorded in Volume 1201, Page 1038, Deed Records, Lee County, Texas (hereinafter referred to as the "Garza Tract"), said 0.924 acres of land, more or less, being more particularly described by metes and bounds as follows:

COMMENCING at an iron rod on the southeast right-of-way line of Private Road 1339, for the west corner of a tract of land conveyed to Laura David in a deed recorded in Volume 1256, Page 903, Deed Records, Lee County, Texas, and for the north corner and POINT OF BEGINNING of herein described tract;

THENCE with the northeast line of this tract and the southwest line of the David Tract, South 47°13'32" East a distance of 317.50 feet to an iron rod found on the northwest line of a tract of land conveyed to Nicolo Achille, Jr., and Cassie Achille in a deed recorded in Volume 1209, Page 872, Deed Records, Lee County, Texas, for the east corner of this tract;

THENCE with the southeast line of this tract and the northwest line of the Achille Tract, South 42°46'28" West a distance of 126.90 feet to an iron rod set for the east corner of a tract of land conveyed to Susan Zoch Ender in a deed recorded in Volume 850, Page 170, Deed Records, Lee County, Texas;

THENCE with the southwest line of this tract and the northeast line of the Ender Tract, North 47°13'32" West a distance of 317.50 feet to an iron rod set on the southeast right-of-way line of Private Road 1339 for the west corner of this tract;

THENCE with the northwest line of this tract and the southeast right-of-way line of Private Road 1339, North 42°46'28" East a distance of 126.90 feet to the POINT OF BEGINNING, containing 0.924 acres of land, more or less.

Being the same property conveyed to Janice Kay McCarty and Rickey Jay Bennett II by Warranty Deed dated December 19, 2022, recorded at Volume 1335, Pages 705–707, Official Public Records of Lee County, Texas, Instrument No. 2022-05101.

The Thessalonian Mandate Institute
Austin, Texas  ·  26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)  ·  EIN 42-2419586
Lease Agreement
Property Lease for Church Seat — 1032 Private Road 1339, Giddings, Texas

This Lease Agreement (hereinafter "Lease") is entered into as of the        day of              , 2026, between the following parties:

Landlord:  Janice Kay McCarty, a single woman
Mailing Address: 5511 Salem Hill Drive, Austin, Travis County, Texas 78745

Tenant:  Thessalonian Mandate Institute, a Texas nonprofit corporation organized for religious purposes under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)
Mailing Address: 5511 Salem Hill Drive, Austin, Travis County, Texas 78745
EIN: 42-2419586
Represented by: Rickey Jay Bennett II, Minister and Chief Executive, acting pursuant to Board Resolution dated May 5, 2026

Article 1 — Leased Premises

Landlord hereby leases to Tenant, and Tenant hereby leases from Landlord, the following described real property situated in Lee County, Texas (hereinafter "the Premises"):

Being a 0.924 acre tract of land situated in Lee County, Texas, being out of and a part of the Drew Champion Survey, Abstract No. 358, Lee County, Texas, more particularly described by metes and bounds in the deed recorded at Volume 1335, Pages 705–707, Official Public Records of Lee County, Texas, Instrument No. 2022-05101, commonly known as 1032 Private Road 1339, Giddings, Texas 78942.

The Premises are leased in their current as-is condition, with no functioning utilities, well, or solar power system as of the commencement date of this Lease. Tenant accepts the Premises in this condition and acknowledges that the absence of functioning utilities is reflected in the rent established herein.

Article 2 — Term

The initial term of this Lease shall commence on                        (hereinafter "Commencement Date") and shall continue for a period of twelve (12) calendar months, terminating on                       , unless sooner terminated or extended in accordance with the terms hereof.

Upon expiration of the initial term, this Lease shall automatically convert to a month-to-month tenancy on the same terms and conditions, terminable by either party upon thirty (30) days written notice to the other party. The month-to-month tenancy shall continue until terminated by either party or until Tenant exercises its option to purchase the Premises pursuant to the Option Agreement executed concurrently herewith.

Article 3 — Rent

Tenant agrees to pay Landlord monthly rent in the amount of                    Dollars ($        ) per month, due and payable on the first day of each calendar month. Rent shall be paid by check, electronic transfer, or such other method as the parties may agree in writing.

Rent payments are made in consideration of Tenant's occupancy and use of the Premises for religious and ministry purposes. Rent payments do not constitute and shall not be credited against the purchase price if Tenant exercises its option to purchase the Premises. Any such credit, if agreed upon by the parties, must be expressly set forth in the Option Agreement or a written amendment thereto.

If rent is not received within ten (10) days of its due date, Tenant shall pay a late fee of                    Dollars ($      ).

Article 4 — Permitted Use

Tenant shall use and occupy the Premises exclusively for religious ministry purposes consistent with the theological mission of the Thessalonian Mandate Institute, including but not limited to: worship, religious instruction, vocational training, prayer, ministry gatherings, and administrative functions of the Institute. Tenant shall not use the Premises for any purpose that violates applicable law or is inconsistent with the Institute's theological mission as set forth in its governing documents.

Tenant is expressly authorized to undertake capital improvements to the Premises during the lease term, including but not limited to the installation of solar power systems, water wells, and related infrastructure, subject to the terms of Article 6 of this Lease.

Article 5 — Utilities and Services

As of the Commencement Date, the Premises have no functioning utility connections, well, or electrical service. Tenant acknowledges this condition and accepts the Premises accordingly. As improvements are completed during the lease term, Tenant shall be responsible for all utility costs associated with the Premises, including but not limited to water, electricity, and any other services made available through the improvement process.

Article 6 — Improvements and Improvement Ledger

The parties anticipate that capital improvements will be made to the Premises during the lease term to bring the property to a functional condition suitable for ministry operations. Such improvements may include, without limitation, installation of a water well, solar power system, and related infrastructure.

All capital improvement expenditures made by either party shall be documented contemporaneously in the Improvement Ledger maintained pursuant to this Article. The Improvement Ledger shall record for each expenditure: the date, a description of the work or materials, the amount paid, the party who made the payment, and the receipt or invoice reference. The Improvement Ledger shall be maintained by Tenant and shall be made available to Landlord upon request at any time.

Landlord's contributions to capital improvements represent voluntary expenditures by Landlord as the property owner. Tenant's contributions to capital improvements on property owned by Landlord constitute leasehold improvements and shall be credited against the purchase price if Tenant exercises its option to purchase the Premises, as set forth in the Option Agreement executed concurrently herewith.

No improvement shall be made to the Premises without the knowledge and consent of Landlord. Consent shall not be unreasonably withheld for improvements consistent with the religious and ministry use of the Premises.

Article 7 — Maintenance and Repairs

Tenant shall maintain the Premises in a clean, safe, and orderly condition throughout the lease term. Tenant shall be responsible for routine maintenance and minor repairs. Landlord shall be responsible for structural repairs and major system repairs that are not attributable to Tenant's use or negligence. The parties shall cooperate in good faith to address maintenance needs as they arise.

Article 8 — Insurance

Tenant shall obtain and maintain throughout the lease term a policy of general liability insurance covering the Premises with minimum coverage of One Million Dollars ($1,000,000.00) per occurrence, naming Landlord as an additional insured. Tenant shall provide Landlord with evidence of such insurance within thirty (30) days of the Commencement Date and upon renewal thereafter.

Landlord shall maintain property insurance on the Premises in such amounts as Landlord deems appropriate. Neither party shall be obligated to insure the personal property of the other party.

Article 9 — Option to Purchase

Concurrently with this Lease, the parties have executed a separate Option Agreement granting Tenant the right, but not the obligation, to purchase the Premises at any time during the lease term or any holdover period. The terms and conditions of any such purchase are governed exclusively by the Option Agreement. This Lease does not create a lease-to-own arrangement, and no rent payments shall be credited against any purchase price except as expressly provided in the Option Agreement.

Article 10 — Default and Remedies

If Tenant fails to pay rent when due and such failure continues for ten (10) days after written notice from Landlord, or if Tenant fails to perform any other obligation under this Lease and such failure continues for thirty (30) days after written notice from Landlord, Tenant shall be in default. Upon default, Landlord may terminate this Lease upon written notice and pursue any remedies available under Texas law.

If Landlord fails to perform any obligation under this Lease and such failure continues for thirty (30) days after written notice from Tenant, Landlord shall be in default. Upon Landlord's default, Tenant may pursue any remedies available under Texas law.

Article 11 — Assignment and Subletting

Tenant shall not assign this Lease or sublet the Premises or any portion thereof without the prior written consent of Landlord, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld for assignments or subletting consistent with the religious mission of the Thessalonian Mandate Institute.

Article 12 — Notices

All notices required or permitted under this Lease shall be in writing and shall be deemed delivered when: (a) personally delivered; (b) sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, postage prepaid; or (c) sent by nationally recognized overnight courier, addressed as follows:

To Landlord: Janice Kay McCarty, 5511 Salem Hill Drive, Austin, Texas 78745

To Tenant: Thessalonian Mandate Institute, Attn: Minister Rickey Jay Bennett II, 5511 Salem Hill Drive, Austin, Texas 78745

Either party may change its notice address by written notice to the other party.

Article 13 — Governing Law

This Lease shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of Texas. Venue for any dispute arising under this Lease shall be in Lee County, Texas.

Article 14 — Entire Agreement

This Lease, together with the Option Agreement executed concurrently herewith and the Improvement Ledger maintained pursuant to Article 6, constitutes the entire agreement between the parties with respect to the lease of the Premises. No prior negotiations, representations, or agreements, oral or written, are incorporated herein. This Lease may be amended only by a written instrument signed by both parties.

Article 15 — Severability

If any provision of this Lease is found to be invalid or unenforceable under applicable law, such provision shall be severed from the remainder of this Lease, which shall continue in full force and effect.

Signatures

The parties have executed this Lease Agreement as of the date first written above.

Janice Kay McCarty, Landlord
Date:                   
Rickey Jay Bennett II, Minister
Thessalonian Mandate Institute, Tenant
Date:

The Thessalonian Mandate Institute
Austin, Texas  ·  26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)  ·  EIN 42-2419586
Option Agreement
Separate and Independent Option to Purchase Real Property

This Option Agreement (hereinafter "Agreement") is entered into as of the        day of              , 2026, between the following parties:

Optionor:  Janice Kay McCarty, a single woman, fee simple owner of the Property described herein
Mailing Address: 5511 Salem Hill Drive, Austin, Travis County, Texas 78745

Optionee:  Thessalonian Mandate Institute, a Texas nonprofit corporation organized for religious purposes under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)
Mailing Address: 5511 Salem Hill Drive, Austin, Travis County, Texas 78745
EIN: 42-2419586

Recitals

WHEREAS, Optionor is the sole owner of fee simple title to the real property described herein, having acquired same by quitclaim deed from Rickey Jay Bennett II recorded in the Official Public Records of Lee County, Texas;

WHEREAS, Optionor and Optionee have entered into a Lease Agreement of even date herewith covering the same property, pursuant to which Optionee occupies the property for religious ministry purposes;

WHEREAS, Optionor desires to grant to Optionee the option to purchase the property on the terms set forth herein, and Optionee desires to acquire such option;

NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of Ten Dollars ($10.00) and other good and valuable consideration, the receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged, the parties agree as follows:

Article 1 — Grant of Option

Optionor hereby grants to Optionee the exclusive, irrevocable right and option to purchase the Property described in Article 2 of this Agreement (hereinafter "the Option"), on the terms and conditions set forth herein. This Option is a separate and independent instrument from the Lease Agreement executed concurrently herewith. The existence and validity of this Option are not conditioned upon the continuation of the Lease.

Article 2 — Property Description

Being a 0.924 acre tract of land situated in Lee County, Texas, being out of and a part of the Drew Champion Survey, Abstract No. 358, Lee County, Texas, more particularly described by metes and bounds in the deed recorded at Volume 1335, Pages 705–707, Official Public Records of Lee County, Texas, Instrument No. 2022-05101, commonly known as 1032 Private Road 1339, Giddings, Texas 78942 (hereinafter "the Property").

Article 3 — Option Period

The Option may be exercised by Optionee at any time during the term of the Lease Agreement or any month-to-month holdover period thereunder (hereinafter "the Option Period"). The Option Period shall automatically extend upon any extension or renewal of the Lease. The Option shall expire and be of no further force or effect upon valid termination of the Lease Agreement, unless the parties agree in writing to extend the Option Period beyond the lease term.

Article 4 — Purchase Price

The purchase price for the Property shall be the fair market value of the Property as of the date Optionee delivers its written Notice of Exercise, as determined by an independent appraisal obtained in accordance with Article 5 of this Agreement (hereinafter "Appraised FMV"), reduced by the Improvement Credit calculated in accordance with Article 6 of this Agreement.

Purchase Price = Appraised FMV − Documented Improvement Credit

The purchase price so calculated shall be the binding purchase price for the closing, regardless of any subsequent change in market conditions. The parties acknowledge and agree that this formula is intended to ensure that Optionee is not required to pay twice for capital improvements it has funded during the lease term.

Article 5 — Appraisal Process

Within thirty (30) days of Optionee's delivery of a written Notice of Exercise, Optionor shall obtain, at Optionee's expense, an appraisal of the Property from a licensed, independent real estate appraiser with demonstrated experience appraising rural residential and agricultural property in Lee County, Texas. The appraiser shall be mutually agreed upon by the parties, or, if the parties cannot agree within fifteen (15) days of the Notice of Exercise, each party shall select one appraiser and the two appraisers shall jointly select a third appraiser whose determination shall be final and binding.

The appraisal shall reflect the fair market value of the Property in its condition as of the date of the Notice of Exercise, inclusive of all capital improvements made by either party during the lease term. The appraisal shall be completed and delivered to both parties within forty-five (45) days of the Notice of Exercise.

Article 6 — Improvement Credit

The Improvement Credit shall equal the total of all documented capital improvement expenditures made by Optionee (Tenant) with respect to the Property during the lease term and any holdover period, as reflected in the Improvement Ledger maintained pursuant to the Lease Agreement.

To qualify for inclusion in the Improvement Credit, an expenditure must: (a) be a capital improvement to the Property, as distinguished from routine maintenance or repair; (b) be paid directly by Optionee and documented by receipt or invoice; (c) be recorded in the Improvement Ledger at or near the time of payment; and (d) increase the value or utility of the Property on a permanent or long-term basis.

Landlord's own contributions to improvements during the lease term do not reduce the Appraised FMV for purposes of the purchase price calculation and are not included in the Improvement Credit. Such contributions represent the property owner's investment in their own asset.

The Improvement Credit shall be calculated and presented to Optionor in writing by Optionee at the time of the Notice of Exercise, supported by the complete Improvement Ledger. Optionor shall have fifteen (15) days to review and object in writing to any line item. Disputed items shall be resolved by the parties in good faith; if not resolved within fifteen (15) days, the dispute shall be submitted to a mutually agreed-upon mediator in Lee County, Texas.

Article 7 — Exercise of Option

To exercise this Option, Optionee shall deliver written notice (hereinafter "Notice of Exercise") to Optionor at the address set forth herein, stating unequivocally Optionee's election to purchase the Property and including the Improvement Credit calculation and supporting Improvement Ledger. The Notice of Exercise shall be delivered by certified mail, return receipt requested, or by personal delivery with written acknowledgment of receipt.

Delivery of the Notice of Exercise creates a binding contract for the purchase and sale of the Property on the terms set forth in this Agreement. Neither party may withdraw from the transaction after delivery of a valid Notice of Exercise except by mutual written agreement.

Article 8 — Closing

Closing shall occur within sixty (60) days of the delivery of the completed appraisal to both parties, at a title company or closing attorney mutually agreed upon by the parties in Lee County, Texas, or such adjacent county as the parties may agree.

At closing: (a) Optionor shall convey fee simple title to the Property to Optionee by general warranty deed, free and clear of all liens and encumbrances except those of record as of the date of this Agreement and taxes for the current year; (b) Optionee shall pay the purchase price as calculated under Articles 4, 5, and 6 of this Agreement; (c) the parties shall execute all documents customarily required for closing a real property transaction in Lee County, Texas; and (d) closing costs shall be allocated in accordance with customary Lee County practice unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.

Title insurance shall be obtained at Optionee's expense. Optionor shall provide Optionee access to the Property for inspection prior to closing.

Article 9 — Title

As a condition of closing, Optionor shall convey merchantable title to the Property, free and clear of all liens, mortgages, deeds of trust, and encumbrances created by or through Optionor, subject only to: (a) easements, rights-of-way, and restrictions of record; (b) ad valorem taxes for the year of closing, prorated to the closing date; and (c) such other matters as Optionee may expressly accept in writing.

Article 10 — Nature of This Agreement

The parties have not entered into a binding agreement to buy and sell the Property until Optionee delivers a valid Notice of Exercise. Article 1 — Grant of Option

Article 2 — Property Description

Article 3 — Option Period

The Option may be exercised by Optionee at any time during the term of the Lease Agreement or any month-to-month holdover period thereunder (hereinafter "the Option Period"). The Option Period shall automatically extend upon any extension or renewal of the Lease. The Option shall expire and be of no further force or effect upon valid termination of the Lease Agreement, unless the parties agree in writing to extend the Option Period beyond the lease term.

Article 4 — Purchase Price

The purchase price for the Property shall be the fair market value of the Property as of the date Optionee delivers its written Notice of Exercise, as determined by an independent appraisal obtained in accordance with Article 5 of this Agreement (hereinafter "Appraised FMV"), reduced by the Improvement Credit calculated in accordance with Article 6 of this Agreement.

Purchase Price = Appraised FMV − Documented Improvement Credit

The purchase price so calculated shall be the binding purchase price for the closing, regardless of any subsequent change in market conditions. The parties acknowledge and agree that this formula is intended to ensure that Optionee is not required to pay twice for capital improvements it has funded during the lease term.

Article 5 — Appraisal Process

Within thirty (30) days of Optionee's delivery of a written Notice of Exercise, Optionor shall obtain, at Optionee's expense, an appraisal of the Property from a licensed, independent real estate appraiser with demonstrated experience appraising rural residential and agricultural property in Lee County, Texas. The appraiser shall be mutually agreed upon by the parties, or, if the parties cannot agree within fifteen (15) days of the Notice of Exercise, each party shall select one appraiser and the two appraisers shall jointly select a third appraiser whose determination shall be final and binding.

The appraisal shall reflect the fair market value of the Property in its condition as of the date of the Notice of Exercise, inclusive of all capital improvements made by either party during the lease term. The appraisal shall be completed and delivered to both parties within forty-five (45) days of the Notice of Exercise.

Article 6 — Improvement Credit

The Improvement Credit shall equal the total of all documented capital improvement expenditures made by Optionee (Tenant) with respect to the Property during the lease term and any holdover period, as reflected in the Improvement Ledger maintained pursuant to the Lease Agreement.

To qualify for inclusion in the Improvement Credit, an expenditure must: (a) be a capital improvement to the Property, as distinguished from routine maintenance or repair; (b) be paid directly by Optionee and documented by receipt or invoice; (c) be recorded in the Improvement Ledger at or near the time of payment; and (d) increase the value or utility of the Property on a permanent or long-term basis.

Landlord's own contributions to improvements during the lease term do not reduce the Appraised FMV for purposes of the purchase price calculation and are not included in the Improvement Credit. Such contributions represent the property owner's investment in their own asset.

The Improvement Credit shall be calculated and presented to Optionor in writing by Optionee at the time of the Notice of Exercise, supported by the complete Improvement Ledger. Optionor shall have fifteen (15) days to review and object in writing to any line item. Disputed items shall be resolved by the parties in good faith; if not resolved within fifteen (15) days, the dispute shall be submitted to a mutually agreed-upon mediator in Lee County, Texas.

Delivery of the Notice of Exercise creates a binding contract for the purchase and sale of the Property on the terms set forth in this Agreement. Neither party may withdraw from the transaction after delivery of a valid Notice of Exercise except by mutual written agreement.
